objective: Become capable of building a small language model from scratch in Rust — no ML frameworks, implemented myself all the way down to the tensor math. The target is a compact transformer-based next-token language model, trained on a small text corpus on a single machine, capable enough to form basic grammatical sentences: greet people, complete simple sentences, and do light grammar correction. I want to understand every layer well enough to implement it in Rust myself: text tokenization (a simple byte-pair-encoding or character/word vocabulary), token and positional embeddings, the transformer decoder block (self-attention, multi-head attention, feed-forward layers, layer normalization, residual connections), the language-modeling head with cross-entropy loss, reverse-mode automatic differentiation / backpropagation and the gradients of these operations, a training loop with an optimizer (SGD / Adam), and autoregressive text generation with sampling (greedy, temperature, top-k). Small / educational scale only on modest data — explicitly NOT large-scale or distributed training, GPU kernel programming, pretraining at scale, or RLHF / fine-tuning.
profile: Working software engineer, fluent in Rust and systems programming, comfortable with data structures and algorithms at the level of a solid CS degree. Remembers early-university linear algebra (vectors, matrices, matrix multiplication) and single-variable calculus (derivatives, the chain rule) but is rusty, and has never worked with matrix / multivariable calculus. No background in machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, or probability beyond the basics.

nodes.work: The Matrix Calculus You Need For Deep Learning (Parr & Howard)
nodes.why: Bridges basic calculus to the multivariable matrix math required to manually derive gradients for your tensor operations.
Teaches how to map tensor math into a computational graph to implement your reverse-mode autodiff engine and core neural network layers.

nodes.locator: Chapter 8: Optimization for Training Deep Models
nodes.why: Provides the mathematical formulations for optimization algorithms so you can write the training loop that updates your model's parameters.

nodes.locator: Chapter 2: Regular Expressions, Text Normalization, Edit Distance
nodes.why: Explains the algorithmic details of Byte-Pair Encoding so you can implement the tokenizer that converts raw text into integer sequences.

nodes.locator: Chapter 10: Transformers and Large Language Models
nodes.why: Provides the complete architectural blueprint of a decoder-only transformer and the sampling logic needed to generate text.
Chapter 6 heavily uses Jacobians and the multivariable chain rule to explain backpropagation, bridging the gap from the learner's single-variable calculus baseline.
Since the learner has no ML background, they must understand the basic training loop, loss concepts, and SGD before Chapter 6 applies them to neural networks.

nodes.locator: Chapter 7: Neural Networks and Neural Language Models
nodes.why: Introduces the foundational neural network components (dense layers, embeddings, softmax) and the next-word prediction framework that the Transformer architecture builds upon.
Chapter 5 formulates machine learning in terms of Maximum Likelihood Estimation and cross-entropy, requiring a foundation in probability and information theory that the baseline lacks.
Introduces the foundational machine learning optimization loop, cross-entropy loss, and softmax classification that neural networks compose and build upon.
Defines the core problem of language modeling, next-token probability, and model evaluation, which is the exact problem Chapter 7 applies neural networks to solve.
